newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's D'Alema says welfare reform or elections.
newsitem.headline: Italy's D'Alema says welfare reform or elections.

text.p: The leader of the biggest party in Italy's centre-left coalition government, Massimo D'Alema, predicted an early general election on Friday if the uneasy alliance failed to agree on a reform of the welfare state.
But D'Alema, head of the Democratic Party of Left (PDS), said the coalition would dump its partnership with the hard left party Communist Refoundation if it had to return to the polls.

His remarks in an interview with La Repubblica newspaper were echoed by Labour Minister Tiziano Treu, who told La Stampa newspaper that Refoundation leader Fausto Bertinotti would be the biggest loser if the government fell.
"If the government takes a tumble because of him, he'd end with broken bones," Treu was quoted as saying.
Refoundation is not a member of Prime Minister Romano Prodi's "Olive Tree" coalition government but ensures its majority in the lower house of parliament.
Its tough opposition to social spending cuts is the prime obstacle to a push by Prodi and his partners to enact structural reform to the welfare state and its biggest component, pensions.

Measures to tackle the issue were absent on Thursday when the cabinet unveiled a 15.5 trillion lire ($9.3 billion) mini-budget intended to ensure Italy's deficit stays within the strict limits needed for membership of Europe's single currency.
Prodi said an eventual welfare reform would be enshrined in the 1998 budget and promised to start negotiations with unions and coalition allies next month.

D'Alema said he did not believe that the current coalition, which took office last May, could be replaced if it fell by a broad-based government comprising some of the parties now in opposition, a scenario that has been the source of speculation.
"It is this majority that has to take Italy into Europe (monetary union) and reform the welfare state. Otherwise we will have to vote again," D'Alema said.
He said early elections would not be with the same coalition.
"How could we go back to voters again with a man like Bertinotti with whom we would have to redo an indefensible deal?," he asked.
Refoundation won 8.6 percent of votes at last year's general election and enjoys influence beyond its size because it holds the balance of power in the lower house.
